newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grains - Indonesian corn demand strong.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grains - Indonesian corn demand strong.

text.p: Indonesian domestic corn demand is expected to remain strong this week encouraged by stable local prices traders said on Wednesday, but grains business in the rest of the region was subdued due to steep rises in Chicago futures.
"Demand is strong, maybe because prices are still low," said one trader in Indonesia.
Domestic corn was quoted steadily at 390 rupiah a kg with the harvest in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra proceeding well, dealers said.
Traders reported no fresh import business after Indonesian feedmills last week snapped up 400,000 tonnes of mostly U.S. corn for delivery in May or June.
U.S. corn on a Panamax vessel was quoted at around US$147 a tonne C&F, up from $145 last week, while Argentine corn was being offered at around $157 a tonne C&F from $155 a tonne last week.
Demand for soymeal was also rising in Indonesia with prices firming in tandem, traders said.
"Local prices have climbed to 825-830 rupiah a kg from 810-820 rupiah last week. This rise is due to the strong demand," one said.
The local market largely ignored news about the looming strike in the Brazilian port of Paranagua which is not expected to affect soybean and soymeal shipments to Indonesia.
Malaysian traders also doubted they would be affected by any Brazilian strike as most of the country's South American corn and soymeal comes from Argentina.

"The local market generally ignored the strike news because our stock is ample. But big feedmills may have to pay attention to price movements abroad because they have to import once or twice this year," a trader in Indonesia said.

Another Indonesian dealer said Indian-origin soymeal was being offered at $320-$322 a tonne CIF, up from $316-$318 tonne CIF last week. Traders recently estimated India had only about 600,000 tonnes of meal available for export.
The Malaysian and Thai feeds and oilseeds markets remained quiet this week, dealers in both countries said.

Weak consumer demand has kept the market in Malaysia subdued, mainly because of ample stocks of corn and other grains following heavy buying before the Chinese Lunar New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr festivals celebrated in early February.
"Buying was heavy before the holidays and most are well covered at least for March," said one trader. "Corn prices are higher but are not rising as much as in the U.S."
Traders said some importers were trying to sell spot maize (corn), but buyers were not interested due to a lack of storage space. Another dealer said the stocks should last until April.
Some traders said they expect the arrival of 1-2 cargoes of corn in Malaysia from China later this month.
Major importers are likely to start looking for forward positions soon, they said.
"This should help support prices in the near term," said a trader at a Malaysian flour mill.

The price of bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in the central region was at 400-405 ringgit a tonne, up from 390-395 ringgit a week ago. "A" grade wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown was at 760 ringgit a tonne. Low grade wheat was at 460 ringgit a tonne.
Imported soymeal inched up to 830 ringgit, from 820 ringgit last week, while local product rose to 820 ringgit from 810.
In Thailand, an estimated 160,000-200,000 tonnes of soybeans will probably enter the market from the end of this month, traders said.

In the soymeal market demand was saturated, traders said. "With some more soymeal coming from India and South America plus local supplies to be available from later this month, we can afford not to buy for some time," said an official at a major Thai feedmill.
Soymeal from India was being quoted around $320 a tonne C&F and U.S. soymeal was indicated at $335 a tonne C&F and higher. Local soymeal was mostly steady at 9.55-9.60 baht a kg.
Corn prices eased this week to around 4.30 baht a kg from 4.50 baht last week due to ample domestic supplies.

"The price of corn eased this week because of rising supplies and lower demand. More supplies are entering the market but the industry slowed down buying as their silos are mostly full after active buying recently," one Thai official said.
